newsitem.title: ALBANIA: President vows Albanians will get money back.
newsitem.headline: President vows Albanians will get money back.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha on Tuesday assured worried investors they would get back cash sunk into creaky pyramid investment funds in a bid to staunch the spread of protests around the Balkan nation.
Berisha was whisked away from a rally of around 6,000 people in central Tirana's Skanderbeg Square after he was nearly mobbed by supporters of his ruling right-wing Democratic Party.
Security chiefs appeared worried and Berisha did not address the crowd directly, although a sound system was rigged up above the steps of the Palace of Culture.
But a presidential spokeswoman insisted there had been no concerns over Berisha's safety.
"He had not been scheduled to make a speech," she said. "It was a symbolic gesture of participating in the rally."
Speaking to Albanian television, Berisha said the government would do all it could to funnel money back to people frightened they will lose all their cash, in some cases everything they owned.
"The government will not only pay back every cent of frozen money of the cheating pyramid schemes but also repair the damage around the country (caused by protesters)," he said.
Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu told a news conference later that total damage had been estimated at around $50 million.

The government has pledged to start the repayments from February 5. Such a promise may have calmed tempers temporarily, but if the banknotes fail to emerge investors were likely to express their wrath once again.

Economists estimate that more than $1 billion may have been plunged into the high-yielding pyramid schemes, which mushroomed across Albania following the fall of the old hardline communist regime in 1990.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has offered to help the Albanian government overcome the financial crisis, an IMF official said on Tuesday.
"The IMF will do everything it can to assist the government in resolving the crisis," the IMF's resident representative in Albania, John King, told Reuters.

Berisha's Democrats, in an apparent bid to avoid any escalation of the violence of the past three weeks following the collapse of the schemes, dropped their original plans to stage Tuesday's rally outside opposition Socialist Party headquarters.

Three cordons of riot police stood in front of the Socialist headquarters, located across from the Palace of Culture, in case the crowd moved towards the rival party building. There was no trouble and the police later left.
Shehu, who is also Democratic Party chairman, alleged the Socialists were operating their own pyramid scheme and said he had evidence to prove it.
In turn, opposition parties have alleged that Democrats used money from pyramids to fund campaigns for national and local elections last year.

The Democrats won a huge victory in controversial elections last May boycotted by the Socialists, and hold 122 seats in the 140-member parliament. The poll was criticised by foreign monitors who said it had not conformed with international standards.
